summary: Gives an overview and explanatory background for the revised IDNA system, covering issues that emerged after the original internationalized domain name protocol was deployed, including keeping up with newer Unicode versions. It is informational and explains the rationale behind the revision.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the story of why the rules for foreign-language website names needed updating and what changed, written so people understand the reasons.

questions: what is the difference between idna2003 and idna2008
why are symbols not allowed in domain names
subtitle: The reasoning behind IDNA2008: why the rules for non-ASCII domain names were rebuilt, and what changed from IDNA2003.

tldr.problem: Years after the original IDN protocol (IDNA2003) was deployed, issues arose, including the need to keep up with newer versions of Unicode, which that protocol had frozen at version 3.2.
tldr.mechanism: IDNA2008 uses an inclusion model based on Unicode properties, drops mandatory character mapping from the protocol, and splits registration from lookup. This RFC explains the rationale and contains no normative material.
tldr.outcome: A few characters such as Eszett and Final Sigma change meaning, which requires transition handling by registries. The RFC is informational and the actual rules live in other documents of the IDNA2008 set.

today: RFC 5894 is an Informational RFC, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It explains the IDNA2008 set, whose definitions are in RFC 5890. The original IDNA2003 specification is RFC 3490.

sections.title: Context and Objectives
sections.content:
Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA) lets client applications convert Unicode strings into an ASCII-compatible encoding (ACE) that is a valid DNS label. The form IDNA uses is the A-label, recognizable by the prefix xn-- followed by characters produced by the Punycode algorithm of RFC 3492. Because A-labels are ordinary DNS labels, no changes to DNS, DNS servers or low-level client libraries are needed.

The first version, IDNA2003, consisted of four documents: RFC 3490, Nameprep (RFC 3491), Punycode and Stringprep (RFC 3454). IDNA2008 depends on none of these except Punycode. The set is listed in the Definitions document, RFC 5890.

The main objectives of the revision were to use a more recent Unicode version and become independent of Unicode versions, to fix a very small number of code point categorizations that caused problems, to reduce dependency on mapping in favor of valid A-labels, and to fix some details of bidirectional handling. This document is informational and normative specifications for conformance appear in the other documents.
sections.plainLanguage: Computers only understand plain letters in website names, so special letters get turned into a plain-letter code that starts with xn--. The rules were old, so they got a refresh.

sections.title: Labels, Registration and Lookup
sections.content:
IDNA2008 introduces terms defined in RFC 5890: U-label, A-label, LDH label, Reserved LDH label (R-LDH), XN-label, Fake A-label and Non-Reserved LDH label (NR-LDH). R-LDH labels have -- in the third and fourth positions. A-labels are the R-LDH labels that begin with xn--, and labels with that prefix that are not otherwise valid are Fake A-labels. The reserved category exists to avoid confusion with pre-IDNA coding forms, to permit future prefix changes, and to reduce opportunities for attacks through Punycode itself.

IDNA does not extend DNS. Applications still see an exact-match lookup service. Adding IDNA to an application needs changes to the application only.

IDNA2008 also separates registration and lookup in the protocol (RFC 5891). That reflects practice in which per-registry restrictions apply at registration but not during lookup, and it helps add permitted character groups without freezing on one Unicode version. Registries are urged to register only exact, valid A-labels, while clients might map invalid user input to a valid A-label.
sections.plainLanguage: Special-letter names get a plain-letter disguise starting with xn--. Shops that hand out names check the rules strictly, while people looking names up are more relaxed.

sections.title: The Inclusion List of Characters
sections.content:
IDNA2008 uses an inclusion model: a code point is invalid unless a Unicode property-based rule, or in rare cases an individual exception, includes it. It divides all code points into four categories.

  • PROTOCOL-VALID (PVALID): permitted, though possibly restricted by context or whole-label rules, such as the Bidi rules of RFC 5893. A registry need not accept every such character.
  • CONTEXTUAL RULE REQUIRED: permitted only where a rule allows it. The best-known examples are ZERO WIDTH JOINER (U+200D) and ZERO WIDTH NON-JOINER (U+200C). The kinds are CONTEXTJ and CONTEXTO, and only CONTEXTJ requires full testing at lookup. A character with a null rule is treated like a DISALLOWED one until a rule is supplied.
  • DISALLOWED: excluded for registration and lookup. Typical groups are compatibility equivalents (changed by NFKC), uppercase and other case-folded forms, and symbols and punctuation.
  • UNASSIGNED: code points with no assignment in the Unicode version in use. They are prohibited for registration and lookup, and move to another category once assigned.

The normative rules are in the Tables document, RFC 5892. Symbols are disallowed because symbol names are ambiguous, for instance several distinct heart characters exist (U+2665, U+2661, U+2765), which makes labels hard to read aloud or transcribe.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a guest list: only characters that are on the list get in. Some get in only under special conditions, some are banned, and unnamed newcomers wait outside until they are given a name.

sections.title: Mapping, Display and Applications
sections.content:
IDNA2003 mapped input through Nameprep, including case folding. IDNA2008 gives no mapping instructions. It assumes the application, perhaps through an operating system input method, maps user input to Unicode code points as it needs, which avoids the two-step mapping of the original protocol. User interfaces are encouraged to map things like uppercase or double-width characters before invoking IDNA, but those mappings are local only. For interchange between systems, U-labels and A-labels must map back and forth without loss.

Applications may accept and display both U-labels and A-labels, but A-labels are opaque and should normally be shown only for special purposes, with the U-label as the default. Display order for right-to-left names is under the control of user agents, and the RFC notes that applications already differ.

Language expectations differ: for example, Norwegian, German and Swedish users treat the ae-ligature, a-diaeresis and the sequences "oe" or "ae" differently. Because IDNA cannot know the language, IDNA2008 treats combined characters in no special way, and registries may apply a variant model or prohibit one form.

For right-to-left text, IDNA2003 rejected labels whose final character needs a combining mark, which breaks languages such as Yiddish and Dhivehi. IDNA2008 removes that restriction with new rules in RFC 5893.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules no longer say how to tidy up what you type. Your app does that, and the system only checks the tidy result, so the plain-letter code and the pretty name always match up.

sections.title: Migrating from IDNA2003
sections.content:
Two design goals drive the migration: applications should not care which Unicode version from 3.2 onward they run on, and new characters and scripts should be added incrementally without heavy processes. A registry can adopt new characters when it chooses. Lookup applications must keep IDNA and Unicode tables consistent, reject only DISALLOWED or unassigned code points and labels that fail a few whole-label rules, and not reject labels on other contextual rules such as mixed-script prohibitions.

A few characters change meaning. IDNA2003 case folded Eszett (U+00DF) to ss and Greek Final Sigma (U+03C2) to medial Sigma (U+03C3), and mapped ZWJ and ZWNJ to nothing. IDNA2008 treats Eszett and Final Sigma as distinct PROTOCOL-VALID characters, and ZWJ and ZWNJ as contextual, so the same string can yield a different A-label. The working group judged this was not significant enough to justify changing the xn-- prefix, partly because a prefix change would force dual lookups, hinder DNS caching and create room for confusion and attacks.

For registries the RFC lists five approaches, such as not permitting the new character, a sunrise arrangement giving priority to existing holders, two variant approaches, or ignoring the issue. IDNA2008 does not use Nameprep or Stringprep at all, so other protocols that use Stringprep are not affected.
sections.plainLanguage: A few letters now get treated differently than before. The team decided that was not worth renaming the whole xn-- system, so each registry must decide how to handle old and new names.

sections.title: Servers, Policy and Security
sections.content:
Existing DNS servers do not know the IDNA rules, so names reach them already converted to A-labels. A-labels are somewhat longer than typical names, so root servers may see a small bandwidth increase and EDNS0 support may become more important to avoid falling back to TCP.

Registries are expected to be conservative about what they register, and lookup applications liberal about what they look up. The RFC also asks registries to restrict registrations, noting that labels mixing more than one script are generally believed to be bad practice.

The IANA Considerations describe an IDNA Character Registry and an IDNA Context Registry, defined in the Tables document, and mention the IANA Repository of IDN Practices of TLDs, which is not IETF-managed. The Security Considerations state the document is purely explanatory and introduces no new security issues, and that trying to implement from it would likely lead to interoperability and possibly security problems.
sections.plainLanguage: Name shops should be careful about which names they sell, while people looking a name up should not be picky. And this document only explains things, so do not build from it.

items.label: PROTOCOL-VALID
items.desc: Permitted in IDNs, possibly subject to context or whole-label rules.

items.label: CONTEXTUAL RULE REQUIRED
items.desc: Permitted only where an associated rule allows it.

items.label: DISALLOWED
items.desc: Excluded for both registration and lookup.

items.label: UNASSIGNED
items.desc: No assignment in the Unicode version in use; prohibited until assigned.
